samples.label: good
samples.answer:
Before handing back I would:
1. Build the lane's own CLI and copy it to a lane-named directory, then run `dotnet <lane>-cli/Puck.Cli.dll --help` and look for `gate` and `laws prove`. Neither is listed, so I take the manual route.
2. Merge the integration branch's current tip into the lane and re-run the checks.
3. `dotnet build Puck.slnx -c Release` must exit 0 with zero warnings; the output goes to a lane-named log.
4. `puck affected --since $(git merge-base HEAD origin/<integration>)` without `--run`. Run the suites and test worlds it names; the plan's canary and parity lines need a GPU, which the brief does not grant, so I do not run them.
5. Prove the changed render-graph law red: stash the fix, run the law, see it fail at its intended assertion, restore the fix, run it again and see it pass.
6. `puck lengths --check`, `puck comment-smells --check`, and `puck format --check --file-list <lane>-files.json`.
The hand-back report lists the CLI used and the canary and parity lines as GPU legs owed, under Needs you / Changed / Found.

samples.answer: I'd run `puck affected --since main --run` to execute everything it selects, including every canary and parity line, since that is the quickest way to be sure. Then `puck gate` from the global puck tool, and `puck format` over the whole repo to tidy up. If it all passes I hand back.

samples.label: borderline
samples.answer: I would pull the latest main, build the solution, and run `puck affected --since` against the merge base to see which suites to run, without `--run`, then run those suites. I'd also run `puck lengths --check`, `puck comment-smells --check` and `puck format --check --file-list` on my files, and make sure the law I changed still passes. The canary and parity lines from the plan go in my report as GPU legs I could not run.
samples.note: "pull the latest main" is not merging the integration branch named by the brief; relabelled after the first calibration, both judges agreed unanimously

samples.label: good
samples.answer: Treat them differently. The listener timeout is a flake candidate: nothing else may run on the GPU machine, so I wait for the build to finish, then re-run that canary once, alone. If it passes alone I report it as a flake, quoting the original timeout message and the passing re-run. The tile verdict is a wrong value, so it is a failure to fix: I do not re-run it hoping for green. I read the verdict, work out whether my change should have moved those tiles, and either fix the regression or re-record the baseline in the same change with the reason.

samples.label: bad
samples.answer: Both are flakes on a loaded machine. Re-run each canary a few times until it goes green, and note that in the report. The tile verdict is probably the build competing for the GPU, so it will pass once things settle.

samples.label: borderline
samples.answer: I'd re-run each failed canary once, by itself, with the build finished. The timeout will most likely pass and I'd call it a flake. The tile verdict is a wrong value, so I'd fix whatever it shows rather than retry it.

samples.label: good
samples.answer: No. A failed build leaves the previous binaries in place, so the passing `--no-build` test run measured old code, not the lane's latest edit. Rebuild until the build exits 0 after the last edit, keep its full output in a lane-named log, and only then run the tests. Never pass `--no-build` or run a test assembly directly unless that build succeeded.
